sections.section_name: Section B - Very Short Analytical Concepts

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Buffer Solution' and provide one standard example of an acidic buffer system. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: A buffer solution structurally resists drastic changes in pH upon addition of small amounts of acid or base. An acidic buffer consists of a weak acid and its salt, like $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$.

questions.question_text: Determine the oxidation state of Phosphorus (P) in Orthophosphoric acid ($\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$) showing the basic calculation steps. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Let the oxidation state of P be $x$. The sum of oxidation states is zero: $3(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$. Solving gives $3 + x - 8 = 0$, hence $x = +5$.

questions.question_text: Differentiate clearly between position isomerism and functional isomerism with brief structural context. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Position isomerism occurs when substituents or functional groups shift positions on the same carbon skeleton. Functional isomerism arises when isomers possess completely different functional groups, like ethanol and dimethyl ether.

questions.question_text: Identify the primary chemical difference between a nucleophile and an electrophile in organic reaction mechanisms. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates an electron pair to an electron-deficient center. An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that seeks electron pairs to form new bonds.

questions.question_text: State Hückel's Rule for aromaticity. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Hückel's rule dictates that a planar, cyclic, conjugated molecule exhibits aromatic stability if its $\pi$-electron cloud contains exactly $(4n + 2) \pi$ electrons, where $n$ is an integer (0, 1, 2...).

questions.question_text: Calculate the structural equilibrium constant ($K_c$) for the general reaction $\text{A} + \text{B} \rightleftharpoons \text{C} + \text{D}$ if the equilibrium concentrations are $[\text{A}] = 0.2\text{ M}$, $[\text{B}] = 0.4\text{ M}$, $[\text{C}] = 0.8\text{ M}$, and $[\text{D}] = 0.6\text{ M}$. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The equilibrium constant expression is $K_c = \frac{[C][D]}{[A][B]}$. Substituting the given concentration values: $K_c = \frac{(0.8)(0.6)}{(0.2)(0.4)} = \frac{0.48}{0.08} = 6.0$. The dimensionless constant evaluates strictly to $6.0$.

questions.question_text: Balance the following specific redox equation occurring in an acidic medium using the ion-electron method: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + \text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+} + \text{Fe}^{3+}$. Show both half-reactions. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Oxidation half: $\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{e}^-$. Reduction half: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Multiplying the oxidation half by 6 and adding yields: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

questions.question_text: Explain the exact inductive effect (+I and -I) using a chemical bond structural example. How does the inductive effect influence the acidic strength of chloroacetic acid compared to acetic acid? [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Inductive effect involves the permanent polarization of a $\sigma$-bond due to electronegativity differences. The -I effect of Chlorine withdraws electron density, stabilizing the carboxylate anion. Consequently, chloroacetic acid releases $\text{H}^+$ easier, making it stronger than acetic acid.

questions.question_text: Draw the detailed structural formulas for all structural isomers corresponding to the molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ that represent strictly alcohols. Provide IUPAC names. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Four alcohol isomers exist: 1) Butan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), 2) Butan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), 3) 2-Methylpropan-1-ol ($\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$), and 4) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol ($\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$). They exhibit chain and position structural variations.

questions.question_text: Provide the complete balanced chemical equations for the following transformations: a) Ethyne to Benzene, and b) Sodium propanoate to Ethane via decarboxylation. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: a) Ethyne passes through a red-hot iron tube ($873\text{ K}$) undergoing cyclic polymerization: $3\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ (Benzene). b) Decarboxylation utilizing soda-lime ($\text{NaOH+CaO}, \Delta$): $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COONa} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3 \text{(Ethane)} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.

questions.question_text: Determine the physical solubility ($s$) of Barium Sulphate ($\text{BaSO}_4$) in pure water given its solubility product constant $K_{sp} = 1.1 \times 10^{-10}$ at standard $298\text{ K}$. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: For $\text{BaSO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}$, equilibrium sets $K_{sp} = [\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = (s)(s) = s^2$. Solving for $s$: $s = \sqrt{1.1 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 1.05 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol/L}$, representing its molar solubility.

questions.question_text: Describe the chemical mechanism of heterolytic bond cleavage using the ionization of tert-butyl bromide as a structural example. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: In heterolytic cleavage, the shared electron pair transfers entirely to one atom. For tert-butyl bromide, the polar $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks unevenly: $\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C-Br} \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+ \text{(tert-butyl carbocation)} + \text{Br}^- \text{(bromide anion)}$ due to electronegativity.

questions.question_text: Read the following case context: An organic chemistry student conducts an electrophilic addition reaction by passing Hydrogen Bromide (HBr) gas into unsymmetrical propene. The primary product isolated is 2-bromopropane, not 1-bromopropane. However, when the exact same reaction is repeated with organic peroxides present, the major product flips to 1-bromopropane. Explain the mechanism behind both distinct results. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Without peroxides, the reaction follows Markovnikov's rule proceeding via a more stable secondary carbocation intermediate, yielding 2-bromopropane. In the presence of peroxides, the Anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch) effect dominates via a free radical mechanism, where the more stable secondary radical leads specifically to 1-bromopropane.

questions.question_text: Read the following case context: A sealed reaction vessel contains a dynamic gaseous equilibrium: $\text{PCl}_5\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3\text{(g)} + \text{Cl}_2\text{(g)}$, where the forward reaction is endothermic. A technician attempts to maximize the yield of $\text{Cl}_2$ gas by manipulating the system. Analyze how increasing the temperature and increasing the total volume of the container will shift this equilibrium according to Le Chatelier. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Because the forward dissociation is endothermic, increasing temperature drives the equilibrium forward to absorb excess heat, increasing $\text{Cl}_2$ yield. Increasing the container volume lowers pressure, causing the system to shift towards the product side (which possesses 2 moles of gas versus 1 reactant mole), further maximizing $\text{Cl}_2$ production.

sections.section_name: Section E - Long-Form Structural & Organic Synthesis

questions.question_text: Deduce the complete relationship between the equilibrium constants $K_p$ and $K_c$ for ideal gas reactions. Start from the ideal gas law and derive the final mathematical expression involving $\Delta n_g$. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: From the ideal gas law, $PV = nRT$, partial pressure $P = (n/V)RT = CRT$, where $C$ is molar concentration. For $aA \rightleftharpoons bB$, $K_p = \frac{(P_B)^b}{(P_A)^a}$. Substituting $P = CRT$ gives $K_p = \frac{([B]RT)^b}{([A]RT)^a} = \frac{[B]^b}{[A]^a} (RT)^{b-a}$. Since $K_c = \frac{[B]^b}{[A]^a}$ and $\Delta n_g = b-a$, the derived relation is strictly $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.

questions.question_text: Provide the detailed, step-by-step reaction mechanism for the nitration of benzene utilizing a concentrated mixture of nitric acid and sulfuric acid. Highlight electrophile generation, sigma complex formation, and proton removal. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Step 1: Generation of nitronium electrophile: $\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{NO}_2^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. Step 2: The electrophilic attack. $\text{NO}_2^+$ attacks the benzene ring, breaking aromaticity to form a resonance-stabilized arenium ion (sigma complex). Step 3: Deprotonation. The $\text{HSO}_4^-$ base extracts a proton from the $sp^3$ hybridized carbon, restoring the aromatic ring to yield nitrobenzene.

questions.question_text: Illustrate the complete step-by-step synthetic conversions for the following chemical transformations: 1) Ethene to Ethane-1,2-diol (Glycol), 2) Methane to Chloromethane, and 3) Propene to Propan-1-ol. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: 1) Ethene reacts with cold, dilute aqueous $\text{KMnO}_4$ (Baeyer's reagent) resulting in direct hydroxylation to form Ethane-1,2-diol. 2) Methane reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ under diffused sunlight ($h\nu$) via free radical substitution to form Chloromethane. 3) Propene undergoes hydroboration-oxidation: reacting first with diborane ($\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$), then oxidized by $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^-$ yielding Propan-1-ol via Anti-Markovnikov addition.
